choices.text: A struct holding a number and a unit
choices.why: There is no unit field. Ninety minutes converted to `int64` was one plain number, 5,400,000,000,000.

choices.text: An `int64` of nanoseconds
choices.why: Right. `1h30m0s` is its `String` method; the value is 5,400,000,000,000 nanoseconds.

choices.text: A `float64` counting seconds
choices.why: `Hours` and `Minutes` return floats, but the duration itself is an integer of nanoseconds.

choices.text: A string such as `1h30m0s`
choices.why: That is how it prints, through its `String` method, not what it is.

prompt: `n := 4; time.Sleep(n * time.Second)` does not compile, while `time.Sleep(4 * time.Second)` does. Why?
hint: What type does `n` have, and what type does the literal `4` have?

choices.text: `time.Sleep` only accepts constants
choices.why: `time.Sleep(time.Duration(n) * time.Second)` passes a computed value and compiles.

choices.text: Multiplying a variable by a duration overflows
choices.why: Four seconds is far from the limit of about 292 years, and the error was a type error.

choices.text: `n` is an `int`, and `time.Second` is not
choices.why: Right: `mismatched types int and time.Duration`. The untyped `4` takes the type it is used with.

choices.text: The `*` operator is not defined for durations
choices.why: It is: `90 * time.Minute` is the first line of `dur.go`.

prompt: To turn the `int` in `n` into a duration of `n` seconds, write `time.___(n) * time.Second`.
hint: The name of the type itself.
Where do the package's units stop, and why there?

choices.text: The space between the number and the unit is the only problem
choices.why: `3days` fails as well: there is no day unit, because a day is not always 24 hours.

choices.text: Its units stop at the hour, since a day's length depends on clock changes
choices.why: Right. The package leaves days to you, where you know which calendar you mean.

choices.text: Three days is longer than a `Duration` can hold
choices.why: A `Duration` holds about 292 years.

choices.text: Durations are parsed from integers only
choices.why: `1h15m30.5s` parsed, fraction and all.

prompt: A program records `start := time.Now()`, and during the next minute the machine's clock is moved back five minutes by the network time service. What does `time.Since(start)` report at the end of that minute?
hint: Which of the two readings does `Since` use?

choices.text: About minus four minutes
choices.why: That is what the wall clock alone would give. `Since` uses the monotonic reading `start` carries.

choices.text: About one minute
choices.why: Right. The monotonic clock only moves forwards and ignores the correction.

choices.text: Zero, because the clocks disagree
choices.why: Nothing reports zero for disagreement; the monotonic reading is used and is right.

choices.text: About six minutes
choices.why: Moving the wall clock back would not add time even if it were used.

prompt: Before writing a `time.Time` to a file, why strip the monotonic reading with `Round(0)`?

choices.text: It makes the file smaller
choices.why: Size is not the reason; meaning is.

choices.text: Files cannot hold more than second precision
choices.why: `Round(0)` keeps the nanoseconds of the wall clock. It removes only the monotonic reading.

choices.text: It is counted from this process's start
choices.why: Right. Another process or machine has a different start, and the number would mislead.

choices.text: The monotonic reading is a security leak
choices.why: The section gives no such reason: the reading is meaningless outside its process.

prompt: What does a timer give you that `time.Sleep` does not?
hint: Where can a goroutine wait for a timer?

choices.text: A channel, to wait on in a `select` and to cancel with `Stop`
choices.why: Right. `Sleep` blocks the goroutine; a timer is a value with a channel and a `Stop` method.

choices.text: Better precision, measured in nanoseconds instead of milliseconds
choices.why: Both take a `Duration` in nanoseconds; precision is not the difference.

choices.text: It sleeps without a goroutine
choices.why: Something still waits on the channel, and that something is a goroutine.

choices.text: It survives a restart of the program
choices.why: Timers live in the process and end with it.

prompt: In `timer.go`, where does the function given to `time.AfterFunc` run?
hint: `main` was busy with the ticker when it fired.

choices.text: In `main`, at its next receive
choices.why: `main` received nothing from it: `AfterFunc` has no channel.

choices.text: In a goroutine of its own, when the time comes
choices.why: Right. It printed at 400 ms while `main` was waiting on the ticker.

choices.text: In the goroutine that called it
choices.why: That goroutine was `main`, and it was still running when the function fired.

choices.text: Inside the ticker's channel
choices.why: The ticker and `AfterFunc` are unrelated; a channel holds values, not running code.

prompt: A colleague's code, in a module whose `go.mod` says `go 1.27.1`, calls `defer t.Stop()` after every `NewTimer` "so the timer is not leaked". What is true of that line?
hint: What changed in Go 1.23, and for which modules?

choices.text: It is required, or each timer stays in memory forever
choices.why: That was true before Go 1.23. Since then an unreferenced timer is collected even if it never fired.

choices.text: It is harmful, because `Stop` drains the channel
choices.why: `Stop` cancels the timer. It does no harm; it is just not what prevents a leak any more.

choices.text: It does no harm and its stated reason is out of date
choices.why: Right. In a module at Go 1.23 or later the garbage collector recovers the timer anyway.

choices.text: It panics if the timer already fired
choices.why: `Stop` on a fired timer returns `false`; it does not panic.

prompt: In `slow.go` the ticker fired every 100 ms for the first 800 ms, eight ticks, and the reader received four of them. How many ticks were dropped?
A program must count every request it receives, and someone proposes counting the ticks of a ticker that the request handler reads. What goes wrong when the handler falls behind?
hint: What happens to a tick that fires while another waits?

choices.text: The ticks queue up, so the count is right
choices.why: A ticker does not queue: `slow.go` lost the ticks at 300, 500 and 600.

choices.text: Ticks are dropped, so the count comes out low
choices.why: Right. A ticker suits "every so often", not counting events.

choices.text: The ticker speeds up to catch up
choices.why: It keeps its period; the late reader finds one tick and no more.

choices.text: The program deadlocks
choices.why: Nothing blocks for good: the ticker drops what nobody reads in time.

prompt: A meeting is set for 14:30 in São Paulo and printed in Tokyo as `2026-10-17 02:30 JST`. What changed in the value?
hint: `Equal` compared it with its UTC copy.

choices.text: The instant moved forward twelve hours
choices.why: The instant is the same everywhere; only the clock on the wall differs.

choices.text: The date was rounded to the next day
choices.why: Nothing was rounded. In Tokyo it already is the next day at that instant.

choices.text: Only the location used to print it
choices.why: Right. `In` changes the location, and the location changes the words.

choices.text: The value lost its monotonic reading
choices.why: `time.Date` never had one; and that is not what `In` does.

prompt: Why compare two `time.Time` values with `Equal` instead of `==`?
hint: What does `==` compare in a struct?

choices.text: `==` does not compile for `time.Time`
choices.why: It compiles; it just compares more than the instant.

choices.text: `==` also compares the location
choices.why: Right. `Equal` said the São Paulo value and its UTC copy are the same instant.

choices.text: `Equal` ignores the seconds
choices.why: It compares to the nanosecond.

choices.text: `==` uses the wall clock and `Equal` the monotonic one
choices.why: The difference is the location, not which clock.

choices.text: Import `time/tzdata`, embedding the database

choices.text: Use `America/Sao Paulo` with a space

choices.text: Set `TZ=UTC` in the container

prompt: Order these durations from shortest to longest.
Which of these are safe ways to measure how long a function took? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which values carry a monotonic reading?

choices.text: `start := time.Now()` before, `time.Since(start)` after
choices.why: Yes. Both readings come from `Now` and carry the monotonic clock.

choices.text: `a := time.Now()` and `b := time.Now()`, then `b.Sub(a)`
choices.why: Yes. `Sub` uses the monotonic readings when both values carry one.

choices.text: `time.Now().Round(0)` before and after, then `Sub`
choices.why: `Round(0)` strips the monotonic reading, so a clock correction in between shows up in the result.

choices.text: Two `time.Parse` calls on printed wall-clock times
choices.why: Parsed times have no monotonic reading, and the printing lost precision too.
